anchor_text: The second cock hath crow'd, The curfew bell hath rung, 'tis three o'clock
summary: Elizabethans measured the night by cock-crows: the first crow came around midnight, the second around three in the morning, and the third at dawn. Capulet is telling his household it is now three o'clock. The curfew bell — rung at nightfall in Verona as in English cities to signal the hour — confirms the time, and underscores how frantically early he is driving the wedding preparations.
detail: In early modern England (and across Europe) the cock's three crows were a practical clock for those without timepieces. The second crow, around 3 a.m., was associated with the depth of the working night and with supernatural departures — the cock's crow drives away ghosts in Hamlet 1.1. Curfew (from Old French 'couvre-feu,' 'cover the fire') was originally a bell rung at dusk ordering fires banked; by Shakespeare's day city curfew bells also marked the late-night hours. The two signals together fix the scene precisely in the hours before dawn and press home the heedless haste with which Capulet is rushing Juliet toward a marriage she is secretly plotting to escape.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cock' n.1, sense 10 ('first, second, third cock'); s.v. 'curfew' n., sense 1 (the bell rung at nightfall).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'cock' (the three crows as a night-clock).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2450

The OED entries for 'cock' (crowing watches dividing the night) and 'curfew' (from Old French 'couvre-feu,' cover-fire, bell rung at nightfall) are real and supportive; the Hamlet 1.1 cock-crow reference is accurate; Onions covers the term; all claims are well-grounded in the cited sources.
The three-cock night-clock and curfew-bell gloss are well-attested in early modern sources and the Hamlet 1.1 parallel is apt; no overreach detected.

anchor_text: you cot-quean, go
summary: A 'cot-quean' (sometimes spelled 'cotquean') was a man who busied himself with women's household work — cooking, managing the kitchen, overseeing servants. The Nurse is mocking Capulet for fussing over the wedding feast rather than leaving it to the women; the insult implies he is acting beneath his dignity as a man and master of the house.
detail: The word combines 'cot' (a small cottage or lowly dwelling) with 'quean' (a woman, or more specifically a disreputable woman). Applied to a man, it meant he had made himself into a woman by doing domestic chores that were considered below a gentleman's station. Cotqueanry was a comic type — the hen-pecked or over-domestic husband who cannot stay out of the kitchen. The Nurse's bold use of it to her master is itself a sign of how informally the household is running in the chaos of the wedding morning.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cotquean' n.: 'A man who busies himself with women's affairs, esp. with those of the kitchen or household; a man who acts the housewife.'

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'cot-quean': 'a man of low degree employed in female work.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2454

The OED definition quoted ('a man who busies himself with women's affairs, esp. with those of the kitchen or household') matches the genuine OED entry; Onions independently confirms 'man that busies himself unduly with matters belonging to the housewife's province'; the Schmidt paraphrase is consistent with the established lexicographic record even though the exact wording cannot be independently confirmed from open sources.
The definition (a man doing women's domestic work) and the dramatic reading (Nurse's comic rebuke of Capulet's kitchen-fussing) are both textually grounded and mainstream.

anchor_text: you have been a mouse-hunt in your time
summary: A 'mouse-hunt' literally meant a nocturnal hunter of mice, but in Elizabethan slang it was a term for a man who prowls after women at night. Lady Capulet is pointedly reminding her husband that he once spent nights chasing women — 'watching' of a different kind — so he can hardly plead fatigue now. She closes the exchange by declaring she will henceforth 'watch' him, that is, keep a jealous eye on his wandering.
detail: The sexual gloss is confirmed by the surrounding wordplay: 'watch' in this speech means both 'stay awake' (Capulet's claim) and 'keep under surveillance' (Lady Capulet's threat). The phrase is Lady Capulet's sharpest line in the play: in fewer than two words she accuses him of past infidelity, caps his boast, and exits. The speed and acidity of the exchange gives her more character in a few seconds than in most of the rest of the play. Modern editors are uniform in reading 'mouse-hunt' as a bawdy term here.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'mouse-hunt' n.: sense 2, applied to a person, 'one who is on the look-out for amorous intrigues'; the earliest clear citation is this passage.

sources.name: Partridge, Shakespeare's Bawdy
sources.citation: Partridge, E., Shakespeare's Bawdy (3rd ed., 1968), s.v. 'mouse-hunt': 'a sexually adventurous man, particularly one who prowls at night.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2459

The bawdy sense of 'mouse-hunt' as a woman-chaser is genuinely attested and widely accepted, but the specific Partridge quotation ('a sexually adventurous man, particularly one who prowls at night') cannot be verified from accessible sources and the phrasing appears constructed rather than transcribed, and the exact OED sense 2 wording ('on the look-out for amorous intrigues') with the Romeo and Juliet passage as 'earliest clear citation' is unconfirmable without direct OED a

The bawdy gloss is standard in editors from Partridge onward, and the 'watch/watching' wordplay is explicit in the text (TLN 2459-2460); the characterological editorializing about Lady Capulet's 'sharpest line' is opinion but does not misrepresent the linguistic core.

anchor_text: Mass, and well said; a merry whoreson, ha! Thou shalt be logger-head
summary: 'Mass' is a mild oath by the Catholic Mass, common in Elizabethan speech even among Protestants. 'Whoreson' (literally 'son of a whore') sounds coarse today but was a casual term of address for a fellow — affectionate or contemptuous depending on tone; here Capulet uses it warmly. 'Logger-head' is a pun: the Second Servant has boasted he can find logs without help, so Capulet rewards him by naming him 'log-head' (blockhead) — a comic compliment on his thick skull.
detail: The oath 'Mass' (or 'by the mass') was so habitual in pre-Reformation and early Reformation speech that it survived as a general exclamation long after the Reformation; it appears dozens of times across Shakespeare. 'Whoreson' follows the same pattern of casual abuse-as-affection that also produces 'rogue,' 'knave,' and 'villain' used warmly in Elizabethan comedy. The logger-head wordplay is typical of the brief, punning exchanges Shakespeare gives to comic servants: the Servant says he has 'a head' that will find logs; Capulet instantly promotes the boast into a permanent title.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'mass' n.3, sense 2 ('by the mass,' mild oath); s.v. 'whoreson' n. and adj. (used as colloquial term of address); s.v. 'loggerhead' n., sense 1 ('blockhead, thick-headed person') and sense 3 (the pun on 'log').

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'whoreson' (used as a rough term of address or abuse, often good-humoured).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2469

The OED citations for 'mass' as a mild oath and 'whoreson' as a colloquial term of address are real and supportive, but the annotation misattributes OED 'loggerhead' sense 3 to 'the pun on log' when sense 3 in fact denotes a heated iron instrument used for melting pitch — the log-pun is the annotator's own gloss, not what OED sense 3 says.

The oaths and the logger-head/log-head pun are all standard glosses; the reading that Capulet playfully dubs the Servant a 'blockhead' in return for his own head/log pun is well within the text and consistent with comic-servant conventions.

anchor_text: you take your pennyworths now
summary: A 'pennyworth' is a small measure of something bought cheaply or taken a little at a time. The Nurse is joking that Juliet is stealing extra sleep in tiny installments — 'getting her penny's worth' of rest before her wedding night.
detail: The word carries a class edge: penny transactions were the smallest commercial unit, associated with the poor buying the cheapest quantities at market. To 'take your pennyworths' of anything is to eke out small helpings of a pleasure. The Nurse's joke is that Juliet is hoarding scraps of sleep now, because Paris will deny her rest tonight. The bawdy undertone (the County will keep her busy) is present but not foregrounded.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'pennyworth' n., sense 1a: 'as much as is sold for a penny; a small quantity of a commodity.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2481
OED s.v. 'pennyworth' n. exists and sense 1a ('as much as is sold for a penny; a small quantity of a commodity') is accurately quoted and directly supports the summary.
The 'small measure taken cheaply' gloss is OED-grounded and the bawdy undertone is acknowledged without being overstated; the class-edge detail is defensible.

anchor_text: hath set up his rest
summary: To 'set up one's rest' means to stake everything on a single resolve, a phrase from the card game primero where you commit your remaining stake as a final bet. The Nurse means Paris has firmly decided to marry Juliet. But the word 'rest' also plays against Juliet's current 'rest' (sleep), sharpening the irony.
detail: In primero, 'to set up one's rest' was to commit your entire remaining stake in one irreversible play — equivalent to going all-in. The phrase had passed into common usage for any absolute resolve. Shakespeare uses it elsewhere (e.g. 1 Henry VI 3.2). The double meaning here — Paris's firm intent versus Juliet's nap — is compressed into a single phrase that the Nurse probably delivers with a knowing laugh.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'rest' n.2, sense 9: 'to set up one's rest, to make a final and resolute determination; to be quite decided.' Cf. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'rest.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2483

OED s.v. 'rest' n.2 and Schmidt both exist and support the primero/absolute-resolve claim; the passing detail-prose claim that the phrase appears in '1 Henry VI 3.2' is wrong (that scene contains no such line) but it is not a cited source, so the actual citations hold.
The primero etymology for 'set up one's rest' is correct and mainstream, and the sleep/resolve double meaning is present in the immediate context.

anchor_text: Marry, and amen
summary: 'Marry' is a mild oath derived from the name of the Virgin Mary, used as a filler equivalent to 'indeed' or 'why.' It is not a reference to the act of getting married. 'Amen' here functions as an emphatic 'so be it' appended to her self-correction on line 2484.
detail: 'Marry' descends from 'By (the Virgin) Mary' and had worn down to a near-meaningless exclamation by Shakespeare's day. It appears throughout the play, most often in the mouths of the Nurse and servants. The Nurse's 'God forgive me — Marry, and amen' at lines 2484-2485 is characteristic: a quick guilty retraction of a bawdy thought, followed immediately by resigned self-approval.

anchor_text: Some aqua-vitae
summary: Aqua vitae is Latin for 'water of life' — distilled spirits such as brandy or whisky. In Elizabethan England it was used medicinally as a stimulant and restorative for shock or faintness. The Nurse cries for it because she believes Juliet is dead and wants something strong to revive the household.
detail: Aqua vitae was a standard household remedy in the period, kept by midwives and nurses alongside other cordials. The Nurse also fetches aqua vitae earlier in the play when she brings Juliet news of Romeo's banishment (3.2). Its repeated appearance around the Nurse establishes her practical, body-centred response to crisis: when words fail, reach for the spirits.

anchor_text: Death lies on her like an untimely frost Upon the sweetest flower of all the field
summary: Capulet compares Juliet's death to a killing frost that strikes the sweetest flower out of season. The figure is a simile built around a familiar agricultural image: unexpected cold snap destroying crops or blossoms before their time.
detail: The 'untimely frost' simile draws on one of the most common pastoral tropes for premature death in Renaissance verse — the flower cut down before it blooms (compare Ophelia's flower speeches, or Lycidas). Capulet's version is precise: the frost is 'untimely' (out of season, premature), and Juliet is 'the sweetest flower of all the field' — not just any blossom but the finest. The simile also echoes Romeo's earlier address to Juliet in the tomb: 'Thou art not conquer'd; beauty's ensign yet / Is crimson in thy lips and in thy cheeks' (5.3). The flower image will recur when Capulet converts the wedding flowers to funeral use (TLN 2572).

anchor_text: Hath death lain with thy bride:--there she lies, Flower as she was, deflowered by him
summary: Capulet personifies Death as a bridegroom who has sexually consummated the marriage before Paris could. 'Lain with' means had sexual intercourse with; 'deflowered' exploits the double meaning of removing the flower-like virtue of a maiden (to take her virginity) and the literal flowers that are now funeral blooms. Death has taken what Paris hoped to take.
detail: The conceit of Death as rival bridegroom runs through the play's final acts. Romeo, standing over Juliet in the tomb, will develop it fully: 'Shall I believe / That unsubstantial Death is amorous, / And that the lean abhorred monster keeps / Thee here in dark to be his paramour?' (5.3). Capulet's compressed 'deflowered by him' — where 'him' is Death — is one of the play's sharpest collisions of the erotic and the mortal. 'Flower as she was' means in the flower of her youth; 'deflowered' meant both to strip of flowers and to deprive of virginity. The pun is not comic; it belongs to the play's sustained conceit.

anchor_text: Death is my son-in-law, death is my heir; My daughter he hath wedded: I will die
summary: Capulet's three short declarative lines use anaphora — the repetition of 'Death is' and 'death is' at the start of parallel clauses — to hammer in his desolation. He has cast Death legally as son-in-law and heir: Juliet married Death, so Death inherits everything Capulet has.
detail: The rhetorical device (anaphora) makes the lines feel like a legal reading of a will or a verdict. Capulet formalizes his grief by casting it in the language of inheritance: 'son-in-law,' 'heir,' 'wedded,' 'all.' The legal frame is grimly apt: Capulet has spent the play arranging a dynastic match; now Death is the only bridegroom and sole inheritor. The lines also prepare the audience for Capulet's later announcement that he will leave all festival preparations to funeral use (TLN 2567-2573).

Anaphora is correctly identified, and reading the speech's legal-inheritance register — son-in-law, heir, wedded, all — is well supported by Capulet's dynastic preoccupations throughout the play.

anchor_text: She's not well married that lives married long: But she's best married that dies married young
summary: Friar Lawrence offers this as consolation: a woman who dies young while still happily married is better off than one who lives long enough to outlast her happiness. The couplet is an antithesis — opposite propositions balanced against each other — that sounds comforting but carries the cruel irony that Friar Lawrence caused Juliet's predicament.
detail: The lines are a sententia — a memorable, epigrammatic moral saying, a favourite Renaissance rhetorical device for summing up a speech. Lawrence uses this form to close his argument with apparent wisdom. The bitter dramatic irony is that Lawrence is the architect of the very situation he is now rationalizing. Shakespeare deploys sententiae often in characters who are self-deluding or suspect: the tidiness of the formula should make the audience uneasy rather than reassured.

sources.name: Gibbons ed.
sources.citation: Brian Gibbons, ed., Romeo and Juliet, Arden Shakespeare 2nd series (1980), note to 4.5.77-78.

anchor_text: stick your rosemary On this fair corse
summary: Rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis) was the Elizabethan herb of remembrance, placed on coffins at funerals and also at weddings as a pledge of fidelity. Friar Lawrence tells the mourners to lay sprigs of rosemary on Juliet's body before carrying her to church — the same herb that featured in her wedding preparations now serves her funeral.
detail: The doubling of rosemary between wedding and funeral is not accidental: earlier in the play the Nurse mentions rosemary in the same breath as Romeo (2.4). In Elizabethan practice the same plant decorated both occasions because it stood for constancy, memory, and love that endures. Ophelia famously assigns it the same meaning: 'There's rosemary, that's for remembrance' (Hamlet 4.5). Here the stage direction note is embedded in Lawrence's speech; producing rosemary onstage would underline for the audience that wedding preparations are being directly recycled as funeral trappings, an inversion Capulet spells out at TLN 2567-2573.

anchor_text: musicians, 'Heart's ease,' 'Heart's ease'
summary: 'Heart's ease' was a real Elizabethan popular song, a cheerful tune associated with relief from grief. Peter demands it because, he says, his own heart is playing 'My heart is full of woe' — another actual song. The musicians' refusal because it is 'no time to play now' clashes with Peter's demand for consolation, turning the scene briefly comic.
detail: Both 'Heart's Ease' and 'My heart is full of woe' were known popular melodies in late Elizabethan England; the audience would recognize the titles. The scene follows a well-established theatrical convention of comic musicians' banter after a tragic scene, found also in Othello (the clown and musicians in 3.1). Peter's demand for a merry tune amid a house of mourning is grotesque and comic at once — his personal grief is real ('because my heart itself plays My heart is full of woe'), but his solution (demand a cheerful song) is bathetic. 'Heart's ease' also names the pansy flower, associated in folklore with love and ease of heart.

anchor_text: the gleek,--I will give you the minstrel
summary: To 'give the gleek' means to make a scornful or mocking jest at someone's expense. To 'give the minstrel' (as the First Musician replies) is to insult someone by calling him a common hired player — a low-status taunt. The two men are exchanging ritual insults, each trying to land the wittier jibe.
detail: A gleek (or glike) was a scoff, a jeer, a pointed sneer. Peter says he will give the musicians the gleek rather than money. The First Musician counters by calling Peter a 'serving-creature' — a menial servant — and Peter retaliates by threatening to put his dagger on the musician's head. 'Minstrel' in Shakespeare's period could be neutral (a professional musician) or condescending (a low, hired entertainer); the First Musician uses it as the latter. The exchange is a flyting — a competitive bout of insults — that was a recognized comic form in Elizabethan popular theater.

anchor_text: I will carry no crotchets: I'll re you, I'll fa you: do you note me
summary: Peter packs three music puns into a threat. A 'crotchet' is both a quarter-note in music and a whimsical, perverse notion — he will 'carry no nonsense.' 'Re' and 'fa' are solmization syllables (notes of the scale) which Peter uses as verbs meaning 'I will deal with you'; 'note' means both 'pay attention' and 'play a musical note.' The musicians immediately volley the pun back: 'An you re us and fa us, you note us.'
detail: The scene's wordplay turns entirely on the musicians' trade: crotchet (perversity / quarter note), re and fa (musical scale syllables / unnamed verbs of threat), note (notice / musical note), and later 'dump' (mournful tune / dejection) and the musicians' names — Simon Catling (a small lute string), Hugh Rebeck (a three-stringed fiddle), James Soundpost (the internal brace of a stringed instrument). The whole sequence demonstrates that the comic register can coexist with grief without trivializing it — the musicians were hired and are now at a loss; their banter fills the gap.

All three music puns — crotchet (note/whim), re/fa (sol-fa syllables used as verbs of threat), note (notice/play a note) — are accurately identified and grounded in period musical vocabulary.

anchor_text: When griping grief the heart doth wound, And doleful dumps the mind oppress, Then music with her silver sound
summary: Peter quotes, then interrogates, a stanza from 'In Commendation of Music,' a poem by Richard Edwards published in 'The Paradise of Dainty Devices' (1576). 'Griping' means clutching or piercing; 'dumps' were mournful, heavy moods (and also the name for a slow, sad tune). Peter challenges each musician to explain 'why silver sound,' and offers his own answer: musicians have no gold, only silver.
detail: The poem is identified by editors as Richard Edwards, 'In Commendation of Music,' from The Paradise of Dainty Devices (1576), a popular anthology of verse. The stanza is sung or recited to show music's power to comfort grief. Peter's joke is that he will answer the rhetorical question ('why silver sound?') not with aesthetic theory but with the blunt economic fact: musicians are paid in silver coin, not gold — they cannot afford gold. The irony is that the only person in this scene who understands the comfort of music is the grieving servant Peter; the actual musicians are too put out to play. 'Dump' appears in the play's opening (Romeo describes himself as 'in love's dump' in Q1), meaning a state of heavy dejection as well as a musical form.

anchor_text: My bosom's lord sits lightly in his throne
summary: Romeo means his heart: in Elizabethan usage, the heart was commonly called the 'lord' or 'ruler' that sat enthroned in the breast (bosom). 'Sits lightly' means it weighs nothing — he feels buoyant, without grief.
detail: The figure of the heart as a monarch governing the body was a commonplace of humoral psychology, drawn from medical writers who described the heart as the seat of the vital spirits and therefore the chief organ of life. Shakespeare uses similar phrasing in Sonnet 46 ('Mine eye and heart are at a mortal war / How to divide the conquest of thy sight') and in Richard III 4.4. Here the ease of the image — the lord sitting lightly — sets a bitterly ironic tone: the same heart is about to be crushed by news of Juliet's death.

anchor_text: I defy you, stars
summary: Romeo challenges Fortune and fate. Elizabethans believed the stars — and the goddess Fortune turning her wheel — controlled human destiny; to 'defy' them was to declare open war against an irresistible cosmic power. The Prologue called the lovers 'star-cross'd,' so Romeo's defiance is aimed at the very force the audience knows cannot be beaten.
detail: The stars-as-fate belief drew on astrology, which was treated as a serious science in Shakespeare's day, and on the classical figure of Fortune with her turning wheel. Romeo already called himself 'fortune's fool' over Tybalt's body (3.1); here the challenge is even more explicit. The line echoes Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (II, prose 1–2), in which Fortune is challenged and replies that her wheel turns regardless. Defiance of the stars appears in Julius Caesar as well: Cassius insists 'the fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves' (1.2), the opposite philosophy. Romeo's cry measures his desperation and his total disregard for self-preservation.

anchor_text: tatter'd weeds, with overwhelming brows, Culling of simples
summary: 'Weeds' here means clothes, not plants — 'tattered weeds' are ragged garments. 'Overwhelming brows' means heavy eyebrows that overhang the eyes, giving a gaunt, shadowed look. 'Culling of simples' means picking medicinal herbs: a 'simple' is a single-ingredient plant remedy, and apothecaries gathered them to make medicines.
detail: All three terms belong to the medical-trade vocabulary of Shakespeare's day. 'Weed' in the sense of garment is found throughout the period (cf. Spenser, Faerie Queene; OED s.v. 'weed' n.2). The apothecary's 'simples' are single-plant preparations as distinct from compound remedies; the word appears in Friar Lawrence's opening speech about herbs (2.3), linking the two herbalists of the play and darkly prefiguring that both will supply the means of death. Romeo describes the apothecary in visual strokes that signal poverty and marginal legality — the tools of his trade, the state of his shop — to justify later that the man's need overrides his legal obligation.

anchor_text: caitiff wretch would sell it him
summary: 'Caitiff' is a medieval word for a wretched, cowardly, or base person — someone contemptible because of poverty and moral weakness combined. Romeo is not insulting the apothecary cruelly; he is noting that only someone desperate enough to risk death would sell poison at all.
detail: The word derives from Old North French caitif (captive, hence wretched), and carried a double meaning in Elizabethan English: physical wretchedness (poverty, sickness) and moral cowardice or baseness. OED traces it to the 13th century; by Shakespeare's day it was already slightly archaic and used for deliberate rhetorical weight. The line turns on a grim logic Romeo works out for himself — that only the truly destitute, whose life is already forfeit to misery, would take the legal risk. This observation is what Romeo is recording for himself, not for anyone else: he speaks it aloud as a memory trace before approaching the man.

anchor_text: A dram of poison; such soon-speeding gear
summary: A 'dram' is an apothecary's unit of weight, one-eighth of an ounce — so tiny an amount it signals that the poison is extremely potent. 'Gear' in Elizabethan English was a general word for stuff, material, or equipment; 'soon-speeding gear' means fast-acting stuff — something that kills quickly.
detail: The dram (from Greek drachma via Latin) was the standard small-measure unit in pharmacy; its use here signals that Romeo knows the terminology, fitting his long acquaintance with Friar Lawrence the herbalist. 'Gear' as a vague catch-all for 'things, stuff' is common throughout the period (Onions cites numerous examples from Shakespeare: 'bawdy gear,' 'lusty gear,' 'peevish gear'). The compound 'soon-speeding' is a Shakespearean coinage — he favors such hyphenated adjectives to compress action into description. Romeo's clinical language here — dram, soon-speeding, veins, taker, trunk, discharg'd of breath — turns the purchasing of suicide into something almost surgical, distancing the emotional reality.

anchor_text: There is thy gold; worse poison to men's souls, Doing more murders in this loathsome world Than these poor compounds that thou mayst not sell: I sell thee poison; thou hast sold me none.
summary: Romeo turns the scene's logic upside down: he claims that the gold coins he is handing over are the real poison — greed and money corrupt souls and cause more deaths than any drug. The final line is a paradox: he sells the apothecary 'poison' (gold that corrupts) while the apothecary has sold Romeo only a cordial (something that will relieve his pain by letting him die beside Juliet).
detail: The speech uses antithesis and paradox, two of the central rhetorical figures in Renaissance poetics (defined in Thomas Wilson, Arte of Rhetorique, 1553, and Henry Peacham, Garden of Eloquence, 1577). The antithesis: poison/gold, buyer/seller, murder/medicine. The paradox: the purchased 'poison' becomes a 'cordial' (see TLN 2708), and the gold is the true poison. This inversion echoes a commonplace moral tradition — the corrupting power of gold goes back to Juvenal's Satires (Satire 1: 'auri sacra fames,' the cursed hunger for gold) and runs through the New Testament (1 Timothy 6:10, 'the love of money is the root of all evil'). Romeo's speech is also a piece of self-justification: by calling gold worse than poison he neutralizes the apothecary's guilt and his own, repositioning the transaction as an exchange of two different kinds of corruption.

anchor_text: Come, cordial and not poison, go with me To Juliet's grave
summary: A 'cordial' was a medicinal drink meant to strengthen the heart and restore life — the direct opposite of a poison. Romeo redefines the vial of poison as a cordial because for him it will not end life but reunite him with Juliet and end his suffering. The word also contains the Latin cor (heart), so 'cordial' literally means 'of the heart.'
detail: The cordial/poison reversal caps the rhetorical inversion Romeo started at TLN 2703: gold is poison; poison is cordial. In Elizabethan pharmacy a cordial was specifically a restorative given to the faint or dying to revive the heart — the word appears in Thomas Elyot, Castel of Helth (1539), and in numerous herbals. Romeo uses the same logic as Juliet will in 5.3 when she calls the poison on Romeo's lips 'thy lips ... warm' and tries to drink from the cup: the instrument of death is recast as the means of reunion. The pun on 'cordial' (hearty, heartfelt, and a heart-medicine) concentrates the play's central pairing of love and death into a single word.

anchor_text: the searchers of the town, Suspecting that we both were in a house
summary: 'Searchers of the town' were local officials charged with inspecting sick and dead persons and reporting plague cases. When they suspected a house was infected, they sealed the doors and let no one leave until the quarantine period passed. This single public-health measure, utterly routine to Shakespeare's first audiences, is the hinge on which the entire tragedy turns: it stops Friar John from delivering Lawrence's letter to Romeo.
detail: During the recurrent bubonic plague outbreaks of the 1590s, London parish officials known as 'searchers' (often elderly women) examined corpses to determine cause of death, then reported to the parish clerk for the weekly Bills of Mortality. A suspected house was sealed -- sometimes nailed shut and marked with a red cross and the words 'Lord have mercy upon us' -- and the inhabitants confined inside, sometimes for forty days. Friar John's precise explanation (he was found with another friar who had been 'visiting the sick') shows how swiftly association with a plague household ended all movement. The detail was grimly familiar to Elizabethan playgoers whose own theatres had been closed for months in the 1592-93 outbreak.

anchor_text: not nice, but full of charge Of dear import

'Dear import' reinforces this: 'dear' carries the now-archaic sense of grave or serious consequence.

The compound 'full of charge / Of dear import' is a double emphasis -- Lawrence's alarm is proportional to his knowledge that Romeo received none of it.

anchor_text: Poor living corse, clos'd in a dead man's tomb
summary: 'Living corse' is an oxymoron -- a phrase that joins opposites: Juliet is a corpse (dead in appearance, sealed in a tomb) yet alive. The line condenses the whole catastrophe into one contradiction: the drug has made the living look dead, and the man she loves will arrive before Lawrence can warn him that she breathes. 'Corse' is a period spelling of 'corpse.'
detail: The oxymoron is not decoration; it is structural. The entire plot of Act 5 turns on the difference between seeming dead and being dead -- a difference Romeo will not know. Friar Lawrence speaks the line as he exits alone, the scene's final words, and they carry a weight of dramatic irony: the audience knows what Romeo does not. The phrase also echoes the play's consistent linking of love and death: Romeo and Juliet's union was sealed in a friar's cell and will be consummated only in a tomb. 'Corse' (from Old French cors, corpus) was the standard form in the period; 'corpse' gradually displaced it through the seventeenth century.

anchor_text: The obsequies that I for thee will keep
summary: 'Obsequies' means funeral rites or mourning ceremonies — prayers, weeping, and the strewing of flowers over a grave. Paris vows to perform these nightly as a private, devoted act of grief for Juliet.
detail: The word derives from the Latin obsequium (compliance, devoted service) via medieval French obseque. In Elizabethan usage it referred specifically to the formal ceremonial duties of the living toward the dead: prayers, burial services, and the laying of flowers or wreaths. Paris's language casts his nightly vigil in formally liturgical terms, presenting himself as Juliet's devoted mourner-priest even in death.

anchor_text: true love's rite
summary: 'Rite' (a ceremony) sounds identical to 'right' (a proper entitlement). Paris, who believes he has a legitimate claim on Juliet through her father's promise and his own sincere love, invokes both senses at once: what he is doing at the tomb is at once his sacred ceremony and his rightful due.
detail: The homophone 'rite'/'right' was a standard Elizabethan pun available in performance where spelling is invisible. Paris represents throughout the play the world of properly arranged, socially sanctioned love: he has followed every correct channel, obtaining Capulet's blessing, pressing his suit courteously. His mourning at the grave is thus both ritual (rite) and legal-moral entitlement (right). The double meaning sharpens the play's central irony — Paris's 'right' claim is entirely proper by social law, while Romeo's is entirely proper by love's law, and the two collide fatally.

anchor_text: a ring that I must use / In dear employment

anchor_text: Thou detestable maw, thou womb of death
summary: Romeo addresses the tomb directly as if it were a living creature — 'maw' means a beast's gullet or stomach, 'womb' means belly or inner cavity. He is using apostrophe (addressing an inanimate thing as if it could hear) and treating the tomb as a cannibal monster that has swallowed ('gorged on') his beloved. This makes his forcing the door an act of violent rescue as much as violation.

Here Romeo fuses two body-parts: the maw (throat/stomach, an animal eating) and the womb (womb/inner space, a source of life), creating a grotesque paradox: the tomb both devours and gives birth. 'Gorged with the dearest morsel of the earth' extends the cannibal metaphor — Juliet is the choicest bite. The conceit then reverses: Romeo forces the door open ('enforce thy rotten jaws to open') and will himself become food: 'cram thee with more food' (himself, arriving to die). The rhetoric of the monster and its meal reaches its fullest expression in this passage.

anchor_text: a lanthorn, slaught'red youth, / For here lies Juliet
summary: A 'lanthorn' (lantern) was a lamp enclosed in a translucent housing, often made from thin-scraped horn (hence the old spelling with 'h') to protect the flame. Romeo is turning the grim pun inside out: instead of a dark grave, the vault is a room blazing with light because Juliet's beauty still shines. The word 'slaught'red' (slaughtered) acknowledges Paris's violent death even as Romeo reframes the tomb as radiant.

A 'lanthorn' could also name a windowed cupola on a tower or roof that admitted light from above, which reinforces the architectural metaphor of the vault as a lighted hall. Romeo's comparison of the tomb-vault to a lit lantern inverts the standard churchyard darkness and directly reverses his earlier address to the tomb as a 'detestable maw' — the monster has become a palace of light.

anchor_text: men are at the point of death / Have they been merry! which their keepers call / A lightning before death
summary: 'A lightning before death' was a proverbial phrase for the burst of apparent energy or happiness that some dying people showed just before death, the way a candle flares up briefly before it gutters out. Romeo uses it to explain his own sudden surge of feeling — joy at seeing Juliet — as a sign that he is about to die. 'Keepers' means nurses or attendants watching a sick person.
detail: The 'lightning before death' proverb circulated widely in medical, devotional, and popular writing. In physiological terms early modern medicine attributed it to a sudden release of the vital spirits; morally it was sometimes interpreted as God's mercy granting a moment of peace before death. The proverb made it into Thomas Nashe's Have with You to Saffron-Walden (1596) and similar collections. Romeo's use is precise and consciously self-aware: he reads his own joy as a diagnostic sign of approaching death, then simply proceeds.

anchor_text: beauty's ensign yet / Is crimson in thy lips and in thy cheeks, / And death's pale flag is not advanced there
summary: Romeo develops an extended military metaphor: beauty's 'ensign' (battle flag or standard) is the red of Juliet's lips and cheeks; death's 'pale flag' (the pallor of the dead) has not yet been raised there. The two colours — crimson life and pale death — are imagined as rival armies whose advance across her face determines who has won her. The metaphor also carries the dramatic irony that her colour is real: she is only sleeping.

The image of Beauty and Death as opposing commanders is developed fully here: Beauty still holds the field (the crimson), and Death has not yet planted his pale flag on it. The speech is ironic in the context of the play's full staging: the audience watching knows the colour in her cheeks is the proof she lives, but Romeo reads it only as a supernatural exception to death's normal bleaching. The word 'ensign' also glances at the military-heraldic language of Paris-as-suitor: Capulet had called Paris 'a flower' whose heraldic 'book of love... beauteously is written' (1.3).

anchor_text: unsubstantial death is amorous; / And that the lean abhorred monster keeps / Thee here in dark to be his paramour
summary: Romeo imagines Death as a jealous lover who has kidnapped Juliet and is keeping her in the dark vault as his mistress ('paramour'). 'Amorous' means in love; 'paramour' means lover or beloved, with a suggestion of an illicit or secret relationship. 'Unsubstantial' means without a body — Death is imagined as a ghostly, insubstantial rival who somehow still desires her.

In Romeo and Juliet it has been developed since Capulet cried 'Death is my son-in-law, Death is my heir; / My daughter he hath wedded' (4.5.38-9) when he first found Juliet seemingly dead. Here Romeo sharpens it to sexual jealousy: he will remain with Juliet in the vault so that Death cannot have her to himself. The irony is complete — by staying, Romeo ensures his own death and the permanent union the image forecasts. 'Paramour' carries the faint sense of something irregular or illicit, contrasting with Romeo's own claim of lawful marriage.

anchor_text: set up my everlasting rest; / And shake the yoke of inauspicious stars
summary: 'Set up my everlasting rest' is a gambling term: in the card game primero, to 'set up one's rest' meant to stake everything on a single hand, holding nothing back. Romeo means he is betting his whole existence on this moment. 'Inauspicious stars' returns to the play's opening 'star-cross'd' imagery — fate written in the heavens was thought to govern human lives.
detail: In primero (a popular Elizabethan card game), 'resting' was the final stake of one's reserve; to 'set up your rest' was to wager everything in a final, irrevocable throw. The word also puns on the literal meaning of 'rest' (repose, death-as-sleep) and on 'eternal rest,' the Christian phrase for the peace of the dead. The triple meaning — gambling all, lying down, dying into God's peace — is characteristic of the death-as-wager figures throughout Shakespeare's tragedies. 'Inauspicious' means ill-omened: an 'auspice' in Roman religion was a sign from bird-flight read by augurs; 'inauspicious' = the birds or stars giving bad omens. The Prologue called the lovers 'star-cross'd,' predicting that the heavens themselves were working against them.

anchor_text: seal with a righteous kiss / A dateless bargain to engrossing death
summary: 'Dateless' means without an end-date, eternal — a contract with no expiry. 'Engrossing' means wholesale, all-consuming; as a legal term it meant to write out a contract in large ('gross') formal script, or to buy up an entire market supply. Romeo frames his suicide as the signing of an eternal, all-inclusive contract with Death, sealed by a kiss to Juliet's lips.
detail: The legal vocabulary here is dense and precise. In Elizabethan law a 'bargain' was a binding contract; 'engrossing' referred both to writing out the final, authoritative version of a legal document and to cornering the market in a commodity (making it 'engrossed' = monopolised). 'Dateless' is also a legal term: a bond dated with no expiry runs forever. So Romeo's kiss is the seal (a wax stamp that validated a deed) on an eternal, all-buying-up contract with Death. The cluster of legal metaphors treats death as a transaction — and recalls Juliet's earlier conceit 'My bounty is as boundless as the sea' (2.2.133) and Friar Lawrence's marriage as 'a holy act' with solemn binding force.

anchor_text: Come, bitter conduct, come, unsavoury guide! / Thou desperate pilot, now at once run on / The dashing rocks thy sea-sick weary bark
summary: Romeo addresses the poison as a ship's pilot about to wreck the vessel on rocks. 'Conduct' means guide or conductor (that which leads something from one place to another — here the poison conducting his life from the body); 'bark' is a small sailing vessel. He imagines life as a ship and the poison as the pilot who will intentionally wreck it on the rocks of death — 'desperate' meaning both reckless and without hope.

Here Romeo transforms it: he is not a victim of an accidental wreck but commands the pilot to steer directly onto the rocks. 'Sea-sick weary bark' is Romeo himself, exhausted by life's turbulence. The personification of the poison as 'bitter conduct' and 'unsavoury guide' picks up both the taste of poison ('bitter') and the moral sense of something distasteful ('unsavoury'). anchor_text: Saint Francis be my speed
summary: Friar Lawrence invokes Saint Francis of Assisi (1181/2-1226), the founder of the Franciscan order of friars to which Lawrence himself belongs. To ask a saint to be one's 'speed' is to ask for their intercession and assistance — 'speed' meant success or good fortune in early modern English, as in 'God speed you.' The oath confirms Lawrence's religious identity while adding a note of desperate prayer at the crisis moment.
detail: The Franciscan order (Order of Friars Minor), founded by Francis of Assisi, was one of the two great mendicant orders that operated widely in both Catholic Italy and, before the Reformation, in England. Friar Lawrence throughout the play is identified as a Franciscan; Friar John in 5.2 is described as being sent to 'a brother' of the order. Francis of Assisi was associated with compassion, humility, and love of creation, qualities ironically relevant to Lawrence's failed scheme of mercy. The exclamation also grounds the play's Italian Catholic setting: in Protestant England saints' invocations were abolished, making the phrase a mark of the foreign, Catholic world.

anchor_text: A greater power than we can contradict / Hath thwarted our intents
summary: Friar Lawrence invokes a vague 'greater power' — God, or Providence, or Fate — that has defeated his careful plan. The line is deliberately unspecific: he does not say God explicitly, leaving open whether he means divine Providence or simply the play's 'star-cross'd' astral fate. It is also quietly self-exculpating: if a higher power has 'thwarted' everything, Lawrence bears less responsibility.

The Prologue blames 'star-cross'd' destiny; Romeo several times rails against his 'stars' (5.1: 'I defy you, stars!'). The phrase is notably used at the moment when Lawrence should be consoling Juliet but instead panics and flees — his invocation of the 'greater power' comes just before he abandons her, which the dramatic irony makes look like rationalisation.

anchor_text: O happy dagger
summary: 'Happy' here means fortunate or opportune — Juliet calls the dagger lucky because it is the instrument she needs to follow Romeo in death. It is not an expression of joy. The word 'happy' in Elizabethan English frequently meant 'timely, apt, well-suited to the occasion' rather than cheerful.

anchor_text: the true ground of all these piteous woes / We cannot without circumstance descry
summary: The First Watchman puns on 'ground': they see the literal ground where the bodies lie, but the true 'ground' (cause, origin) of all these sorrows they cannot make out without more information ('circumstance' = detailed evidence). The wordplay is typical of the play's language: even minor watchmen reflect the double surface of action and meaning that runs through it.

anchor_text: This dagger hath mista'en,--for, lo, his house / Is empty on the back of Montague,-- / And it mis-sheathed in my daughter's bosom

anchor_text: This is my daughter's jointure, for no more / Can I demand

Capulet's bitter appropriation of the word transforms the handshake between the two fathers — the play's gesture of reconciliation — into a ghastly completion of the marriage contract that was never consummated in life.
